     24	---
     25	# Amazon EBS Expertise
     26	
     27	Use this skill to troubleshoot Amazon EBS problems and to review an account's Amazon EBS setup. It has two modes. Troubleshoot mode answers "something is wrong, why?" through one of five paths and returns a fixed verdict. Review mode answers "is my EBS setup healthy before something goes wrong?" and returns a rated report. Both modes are read-only and share the same volume-type rules, instance limits and service rules. Load only the reference files the request needs.
     28	
     29	## When to Use This Skill
     30	
     31	- Storage-related slowness, timeouts or high I/O latency on an Amazon EC2 instance.
     32	- An alarm on AWS/EBS metrics or on instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%`.
     33	- A request to raise IOPS or throughput, or to modify a volume.
     34	- A volume modification that looks stuck, failed, or did not improve performance.
     35	- Snapshot, AMI, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, AWS Backup or Recycle Bin questions, including which snapshots need owner review before deletion.
     36	- Encrypted-volume access errors and AWS KMS questions for Amazon EBS.
     37	- Amazon EBS cost increases, idle or over-provisioned volumes.
     38	- An operation that failed on an Amazon EBS quota, or "how close am I to my limits?"
     39	- A request to review Amazon EBS posture before a launch, migration or peak event.
     40	
     41	Do not use this skill for Amazon S3, Amazon EFS, Amazon FSx, instance store, or Amazon EC2 issues unrelated to Amazon EBS.
     42	
     43	## Prerequisites
     44	
     45	- Read-only permissions for the APIs listed in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md).
     46	- AWS CloudTrail access is optional. The skill works without it.
     47	- Mutating changes run only through directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App), which need their own role and operator approval on the approval card.
     48	
     49	---
     50	
     51	## Workflow
     52	
     53	Copy this checklist and tick each step as you finish it:
     54	
     55	- [ ] Step 1: Classify the request
     56	- [ ] Step 2: Load the shared references
     57	- [ ] Step 3: Run the path and draft the report
     58	- [ ] Step 4: Check the draft, fix it, then present it
     59	
     60	## Step 1: Classify the Request
     61	
     62	| The user says or the alarm shows | Mode and path | Load |
     63	|---|---|---|
     64	| "My app is slow", high latency, an alarm on AWS/EBS metrics, `EBSIOBalance%` or `EBSByteBalance%`, "is it storage?", "how much IOPS do I need?" | Troubleshoot: performance | [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md) |
     65	| "My modification is stuck", "the new IOPS has not taken effect", a `ModifyVolume` error, resize, gp2 to gp3, extend the file system, shrink or cancel | Troubleshoot: volume modification | [references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md](references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md) |
     66	| "Which snapshots can I delete?", snapshot copy did not arrive, AMI creation stuck, recover a deleted snapshot or volume, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, Recycle Bin | Troubleshoot: snapshots | [references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md](references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md) |
     67	| "I can't attach my KMS-encrypted volume", share an encrypted snapshot or AMI, encryption by default, re-encrypt a volume | Troubleshoot: encryption | [references/troubleshoot-encryption.md](references/troubleshoot-encryption.md) |
     68	| "Why did my EBS bill go up?", unexplained charges, idle or unattached volumes, pricing model | Troubleshoot: billing | [references/troubleshoot-billing.md](references/troubleshoot-billing.md) |
     69	| "Limit exceeded", a quota error, "how close am I to my limits?" | Shared capability: quota headroom | [Capacity and quota headroom](references/review-operational.md#capacity-and-quota-headroom) |
     70	| "Are my volumes backed up?" | Review: resilience area | [Resilience](references/review-operational.md#resilience) |
     71	| "Review my EBS setup", "is my storage production-ready?" | Review | [references/review-operational.md](references/review-operational.md) and [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md) |
     72	
     73	If a request fits more than one row, answer the question the user asked first and treat the rest as Separate findings.
     74	
     75	## Step 2: Load the Shared References
     76	
     77	- Always load [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md) (read-only APIs, metric math, errors and fallbacks).
     78	- Load [references/metrics-thresholds.md](references/metrics-thresholds.md) for any metric judgement.
     79	- Load [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md) for the verdict, the binding layer, escalation and review ratings.
     80	- Load [references/ebs-best-practices.md](references/ebs-best-practices.md) for service rules (Elastic Volumes, instance limits, quotas, snapshots, quirks).
     81	
     82	## Step 3: Run the Path and Draft the Report
     83	
     84	Follow the numbered procedure in the loaded path. Discover every value from the APIs. Then draft the report in the format below.
     85	
     86	### Troubleshoot verdict format
     87	
     88	1. **Answer:** the asked question, answered first.
     89	2. **Evidence:** values with units and time window.
     90	3. **Binding layer:** Volume, Instance, Burst credits, Quota, Not EBS, AWS-side impairment (only with a direct signal, see [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md)), Indeterminate, or Not applicable.
     91	4. **Recommendation:** exact parameters, or "No change".
     92	5. **Separate findings:** other true facts that do not change the Answer.
     93	6. **Gaps:** what could not be checked and why.
     94	
     95	In an investigation, put the Answer and the Recommendation with its exact parameters in the root cause finding, not only under Gaps. Keep the findings on the resource the user asked about. Mention another volume only when it shares the same instance EBS baseline, and then as a Separate finding.
     96	
     97	When the Binding layer is Indeterminate, report it as one finding. Do not offer AWS-side impairment as a hypothesis. List each direct check you ran (volume status, `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, AWS Health, AWS FIS) with its result as supporting evidence, say that no check confirms or rules out an EBS-side slowdown, and give the escalation path.
     98	
     99	Review mode uses the rated report in [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md). Every Review mode response MUST begin with its Summary table, which rates all six areas (capacity and quota headroom, observability, cost hygiene, resilience, encryption posture, deletion protection), even when an area has no findings or is `Indeterminate`. The Summary table is required, not optional. Do not open with prose or an offer to run the review; start with the table, then the per-area detail.
     100	
     101	## Step 4: Check the Draft Before Presenting It
     102	
     103	Review the draft from Step 3 against these checks. Fix anything that fails, then present it.
     104	
     105	- Every number under Evidence came from an API call made in this session, has its unit and time window, and matches the resource ID it is attributed to.
     106	- The Binding layer agrees with the Evidence: the named layer is the one at its limit, and the other layers were checked and shown to have headroom. The Evidence gives the instance EBS baseline in MiB/s and IOPS next to the summed demand of all attached volumes.
     107	- Any Recommendation stays within the instance's EBS baseline and the volume type's documented limits, and it is not more provisioning for an impairment.
     108	- Every snapshot tier is backed by the checks it requires; if one of those checks failed, the item is not listed for owner review. No snapshot is recommended for deletion; the owner confirms first.
     109	- A review answer starts with the Summary table and rates all six areas.
     110	- Every API that failed or was not called is listed under Gaps.
     111	
     112	---
     113	
     114	## Critical Rules
     115	
     116	- **Read-only.** Changes (ModifyVolume, quota requests) are proposed with exact parameters, cost and rollback, and run only through operator-approved directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App). Approval is given only on the approval card. A typed "approve" in chat is not approval.
     117	- **Deletes are manual customer steps.** AWS DevOps Agent refuses delete-class operations (for example DeleteSnapshot, DeleteVolume, DeregisterImage), so never propose them as directed actions. After the owner confirms they no longer need the resource, give the commands for the customer to run with their own credentials.
     118	- **Answer in one reply.** In chat, run the checks in this conversation and return the finished verdict or report as your reply. Do not hand the work to a background sub-agent and reply with a "started" or "I will report back" message, because that message becomes the answer the user sees first.
     119	- **Discover, don't assume:** read every configuration value from the APIs.
     120	- **Rule EBS in or out before tuning it.**
     121	- **Answer the asked question first;** other findings go under "Separate findings".
     122	- **Review mode starts with the Summary table.** Every Review mode response begins with the Summary table of all six rated areas. The table is required, not optional.
     123	- **Always check the instance layer** and size changes within the instance's EBS **baseline**.
     124	- **Never recommend more provisioning for an impairment.**
     125	- **Use current service rules:** up to 4 Elastic Volumes modifications per volume per rolling 24 hours. There is no fixed waiting period between modifications; the next one is allowed once the previous one completes.
     126	- **No interpretation without data:** report what couldn't be checked and use fallbacks. `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the most recent modification per volume; modification history and counts come from the optional AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` events, or are listed under Gaps.
     127	- **Units:** MiB/s for throughput, stated every time.
     128	- **Escalate** on scope signals or when the investigation can't explain the symptom.
     129	
     130	## Gotchas
     131	
     132	- A modification in `optimizing` is not stuck. The new size, IOPS or throughput already applies while it optimizes.
     133	- `DescribeInstanceTypes` reports EBS bandwidth in MB/s. Convert it to MiB/s before comparing it with volume throughput.
     134	- On io1 and io2, `VolumeThroughputPercentage` is the percentage of provisioned IOPS delivered. It is not a throughput signal.
     135	- `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` need both `VolumeId` and `InstanceId` and exist only on Nitro instances. `VolumeAvgThroughput` is in KiB/s. `VolumeTotalReadTime` and `VolumeTotalWriteTime` are in seconds.
     136	- Rising latency and queue length with falling IOPS is not proof of an AWS-side impairment. Without a direct signal (failed `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, impaired volume status, or an open AWS Health event) and without a running AWS FIS experiment, the Binding layer is Indeterminate.
     137	- `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the latest modification per volume. It cannot count modifications in the last 24 hours.
     138	- `ListRecoveryPointsByResource` without `ManagedByAWSBackupOnly` set to true also lists snapshots that AWS Backup did not create.
     139	- A snapshot whose source volume is gone may be the only remaining copy of the data. List it for owner review; never call it safe to delete.
     140	- Snapshots are incremental, so deleting one may free less storage than its size suggests.
     141	
     142	## Error Handling
     143	
     144	Errors, gated reads and missing metrics are handled with the fallback table in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md). Name every failed API under Gaps and continue with the rest.
     145	
     146	## References
     147	
     148	- [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md): performance attribution, the live-tested procedure
     149	- [references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md](references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md): snapshot tiers (owner review), copy, AMI, lifecycle and recovery
     150	- [references/troubleshoot-encryption.md](references/troubleshoot-encryption.md): AWS KMS access, sharing encrypted snapshots, default encryption
     151	- [references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md](references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md): modification states, limits, errors, sizing, file system extension
     152	- [references/troubleshoot-billing.md](references/troubleshoot-billing.md): cost breakdown, change records, right-sizing
     153	- [references/review-operational.md](references/review-operational.md): Review mode checks and the quota headroom capability
     154	- [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md): read-only API allowlist, metric math, errors, fallbacks
     155	- [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md): verdict template, binding layer, escalation, review ratings
     156	- [references/metrics-thresholds.md](references/metrics-thresholds.md): documented limits and how to judge each volume type
     157	- [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md): rated report layout for Review mode
     158	- [references/ebs-best-practices.md](references/ebs-best-practices.md): volume-type rules, quotas, Elastic Volumes rules, quirks"}], "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}], "user_reference": null}

{"id": "63e93b26-2358-407d-95fe-1852c5f43e56", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_jDm2ZRaZouFYiaiqo0F0Gd", "content": [{"text": "     1	# Troubleshoot: performance attribution
     2	
     3	## When this path applies
     4	
     5	- The user reports slowness, timeouts or high I/O latency on an instance or application.
     6	- A CloudWatch alarm fired on AWS/EBS metrics (`VolumeReadOps`, `VolumeWriteOps`, `VolumeReadBytes`, `VolumeWriteBytes`, `VolumeQueueLength`, `VolumeTotalReadTime`, `VolumeTotalWriteTime`, `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `BurstBalance`) or on instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%`.
     7	- A volume modification did not improve performance.
     8	- The user asks how much IOPS or throughput to provision.
     9	
     10	## Procedure
     11	
     12	Discover everything from the alarm. Do not assume volume type, size, provisioned values, instance type, or tags; read them from the APIs.
     13	
     14	### Step 1: Identify the alarmed volume(s)
     15	
     16	- Get the alarm and its state history (when it first entered ALARM).
     17	- Extract VolumeId from the alarm's metric dimensions. For metric-math alarms, read the VolumeId from each metric in the expression.
     18	- If the alarm is on an instance metric (EBSIOBalance%, EBSByteBalance%), start from the InstanceId instead.
     19	- If there is no alarm (a chat request such as "my app is slow"), start from the InstanceId the user gives, or ask for it.
     20	
     21	### Step 2: Build the context
     22	
     23	- DescribeVolumes on the alarmed volume: VolumeType, Size, Iops, Throughput, attachment InstanceId, tags (for naming only).
     24	- DescribeInstances + DescribeInstanceTypes for that instance: instance type and its EBS baseline/maximum bandwidth (MiB/s) and IOPS.
     25	- List ALL volumes attached to that instance (they share instance EBS bandwidth). Investigate this set, not the whole account.
     26	- `DescribeInstanceTypes` reports throughput in MB/s. Convert to MiB/s before any comparison (see [data-collection.md](data-collection.md)).
     27	- Always run `DescribeVolumeStatus` for every attached volume (volume status, status checks, scheduled events), whatever the alarm or request. Record the result as evidence. An impaired status or a failing check is a scope signal for escalation (see [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md)), but still finish Steps 3 to 5.
     28	
     29	### Step 2b: Rule EBS in or out (chat requests with no EBS alarm only)
     30	
     31	This check runs only when the run did not start from an AWS/EBS alarm or an `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%` alarm, for example a chat request such as "my app is slow, is it storage?". When an EBS alarm triggered the run, skip this step and run Steps 3 to 6 in full.
     32	
     33	Read `CPUUtilization` for the instance, and the latency, `VolumeQueueLength`, `BurstBalance` (gp2, st1, sc1) and instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%` (if published) for the volumes found in Step 2, over the same window. Use the qualitative attribution matrix in [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md). Report "Not EBS" and stop tuning storage only if all of these hold: CPU is high, volume latency and queue length are normal, no `DescribeVolumeStatus` problem was found, and no burst or instance balance is draining or at 0. Otherwise continue with Step 3.
     34	
     35	### Step 3: Measure each volume on the dimension(s) its type is limited by
     36	
     37	Pull the last 30 minutes of AWS/EBS metrics at 1-minute granularity.
     38	
     39	- Actual IOPS = (VolumeReadOps + VolumeWriteOps) / period seconds
     40	- Actual throughput = (VolumeReadBytes + VolumeWriteBytes) / period, in MiB/s
     41	- Avg latency in ms per operation = Sum(VolumeTotalReadTime) / Sum(VolumeReadOps) x 1,000, and the same for writes with VolumeTotalWriteTime and VolumeWriteOps. VolumeTotalReadTime and VolumeTotalWriteTime are in seconds, so the x 1,000 converts to milliseconds. `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` are already in milliseconds
     42	- VolumeQueueLength
     43	- `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` need both dimensions, `VolumeId` AND `InstanceId`, and exist only on Nitro instances. `VolumeAvgThroughput` is in KiB/s; divide by 1,024 for MiB/s. `VolumeQueueLength` uses `VolumeId` only. If `VolumeAvg*` returns nothing, use the Sum-based math above.
     44	- Always read `VolumeIdleTime` (seconds in the period with no read or write submitted; `VolumeId` only). Idle percentage = Sum(`VolumeIdleTime`) / period seconds x 100. Report it as evidence for every volume. Near 0 means I/O was submitted for the whole period, which fits both saturation and impairment, so use Step 5 to tell them apart. A volume that is mostly idle during the alarm window is unlikely to be the binding volume. There is no fixed band; compare with the volume's own history.
     45	
     46	Apply the rule for the volume's type:
     47	
     48	- gp3: IOPS and throughput are provisioned independently. Compare actual IOPS to Iops AND actual MiB/s to Throughput; either can bind.
     49	- gp2: baseline IOPS = 3 x GiB (min 100), burst to 3,000 while BurstBalance > 0. Check BurstBalance draining or at 0.
     50	- io1/io2 (incl. Block Express): compare actual IOPS to provisioned Iops AND actual MiB/s to the volume's throughput limit; either can bind. Throughput is not provisioned separately, but the documented throughput limit depends on the provisioned IOPS (see the io1 and io2 rows in [metrics-thresholds.md](metrics-thresholds.md)). Compute the limit from `Iops` with those rules, then compare. Do NOT use VolumeThroughputPercentage to judge throughput on io1/io2; it reports the % of provisioned IOPS delivered.
     51	- st1/sc1: throughput-oriented with burst credits; compare MiB/s to the baseline/burst for the size and check BurstBalance.
     52	- Judge io1, io2 and gp3 by both IOPS and throughput. Per-type limits are in [metrics-thresholds.md](metrics-thresholds.md).
     53	
     54	### Step 4: Check the instance layer
     55	
     56	- Sum actual IOPS and MiB/s across all attached volumes; compare to the instance type's EBS baseline from DescribeInstanceTypes.
     57	- Aggregate across ALL attached volumes, including the root volume.
     58	- Check EBSIOBalance% / EBSByteBalance%. If they are draining or at 0, or the sum is at the instance limit, the INSTANCE is the binding layer and raising volume provisioning will not help.
     59	- If instance metrics are healthy and a volume is at its own limit, the VOLUME is the binding layer.
     60	- If `EBSIOBalance%` is absent, the instance size does not publish it. Use the summed values against the baseline.
     61	
     62	### Step 5: Distinguish saturation from impairment
     63	
     64	If queue length and latency are elevated but the volume and instance are both below their limits, this is NOT saturation. Suspect an impairment or injected latency; do NOT recommend increasing provisioning.
     65	
     66	The impairment signature is IOPS and throughput collapsing while latency and `VolumeQueueLength` rise. Saturation looks different: metrics flat at the provisioned limit with modest latency. When you see the impairment signature, check in this order:
     67	
     68	1. The `DescribeVolumeStatus` result from Step 2 (impaired status, failing checks, scheduled events). Read it again if the symptom started after Step 2.
     69	2. The `VolumeStalledIOCheck` metric for the volume (dimensions `VolumeId` AND `InstanceId`, Nitro instances only; 0 passed, 1 failed). A failed check (value 1) means the volume's IO is stalled, which is an AWS-side impairment. Escalate per the rules in [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md) and never recommend adding IOPS.
     70	3. AWS Health `DescribeEvents` for Amazon EBS and Amazon EC2 events in the Region and Availability Zone.
     71	4. AWS FIS `ListExperiments` for a running experiment that targets the volume or instance, with actions `aws:ebs:volume-io-latency` or `aws:ebs:pause-volume-io`. If one is running, say so plainly: the latency is injected and will end with the experiment.
     72

     95	
     96	### Micro-bursting
     97	
     98	AWS/EBS data is 1-minute. Sub-minute peaks can reach a limit while the minute average stays below it. If latency or queue length rises while the average is below the limit, say that micro-bursting is possible and that headroom is not proven. Do not claim headroom from the average alone.

     102	A volume created from a snapshot loads blocks from Amazon S3 the first time they are read, which adds latency until the volume is initialized.      3	## Troubleshoot verdict template
     4	
     5	Every troubleshoot answer uses these six headings in this order.
     6	
     7	1. **Answer.** The question the user asked, answered first in one or two sentences. For example "Not stuck. The modification is in `optimizing`, which already applies the new IOPS."
     8	2. **Evidence.** The values that support the answer, each with units and the time window (for example "average `<value>` IOPS, `<start>` to `<end>` UTC"). Throughput in MiB/s.
     9	3. **Binding layer.** One of: Volume, Instance, Burst credits, Quota, Not EBS, AWS-side impairment, Indeterminate, Not applicable.
     10	4. **Recommendation.** Exact parameters (volume ID, dimension, target value, how the target was computed), or "No change". Mutating steps are proposals for a directed action.
     11	5. **Separate findings.** Other true facts, labelled so they never change the Answer. For example a modification that succeeded on a volume whose instance caps delivered IOPS: the cap goes here, never as "the modification failed".
     12	6. **Gaps.** What could not be checked and why (API denied, approval gate, metric absent).

     14	## Binding-layer decision tree
     15	
     16	Work through it in order. Use measured values and the limits read from the APIs. Do not use fixed percentage triggers.

     23	
     24	## Metric rules
     25	
     26	AWS/EBS publishes 1-minute data.
     27	
     28	| Namespace | Metrics | Dimensions |
     29	|---|---|---|
     30	| AWS/EBS | `VolumeAvgIOPS` (Ops/s), `VolumeAvgThroughput` (KiB/s), `VolumeAvgReadLatency` (milliseconds), `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` (milliseconds), `VolumeStalledIOCheck` (0 passed, 1 failed) | `VolumeId` AND `InstanceId`. Nitro instances only |
     31	| AWS/EBS | `VolumeReadOps`, `VolumeWriteOps`, `VolumeReadBytes`, `VolumeWriteBytes`, `VolumeTotalReadTime` (seconds), `VolumeTotalWriteTime` (seconds), `VolumeQueueLength`, `VolumeIdleTime` (seconds), `BurstBalance`, `VolumeThroughputPercentage` (Provisioned IOPS SSD only) | `VolumeId` |
     32	| AWS/EC2 | `EBSIOBalance%`, `EBSByteBalance%`, `EBSReadOps`, `EBSWriteOps`, `EBSReadBytes`, `EBSWriteBytes` | `InstanceId` |
     33	
     34	Metric math from the Amazon CloudWatch metrics page for Amazon EBS. Use `Sum` statistics for ops, bytes and time.
     35	
     36	- IOPS = Sum(`VolumeReadOps` + `VolumeWriteOps`) / period in seconds
     37	- MiB/s = Sum(`VolumeReadBytes` + `VolumeWriteBytes`) / period in seconds / 1,048,576
     38	- Average read latency in milliseconds per operation = Sum(`VolumeTotalReadTime`, in seconds) / Sum(`VolumeReadOps`) x 1,000 (and the write equivalent with `VolumeTotalWriteTime` and `VolumeWriteOps`). Without the x 1,000 the result is in seconds. Always state latency in milliseconds
     39	- Idle percentage = Sum(`VolumeIdleTime`) / period in seconds x 100
     40	- MiB/s from `VolumeAvgThroughput` = value in KiB/s / 1,024
     41	
     42	What a 1-minute average hides: sub-minute peaks can reach a limit while the minute average looks below it (micro-bursting). When latency or queue length rises while the average sits below the limit, say that headroom is not proven instead of claiming it.
     43	
     44	`EBSIOBalance%` and `EBSByteBalance%` are published only for some instance sizes (generally 4xlarge and smaller) that can burst. If they are absent, the instance does not publish them. That is not a fault.

Record a Gap for the modification history and for the 24-hour modification count |

{"id": "9d0fb9ddaacb41419dc069b50ef00996", "role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Fast agent report: a separate fast agent investigated this same incident in parallel and has finished. This is its whole final report, shared once. Nobody has checked it.

## Root cause
The bottleneck is the volume itself, specifically its provisioned IOPS. The volume, vol-0123456789abcdef0, is a 10 GiB io2 volume provisioned at 1,000 IOPS. Around 16:15 UTC a sustained stream of small writes (about 8 KiB each) started, and from 16:20 the volume has done almost exactly 300,000 writes every 5 minutes. That is 1,000 IOPS, the provisioned limit, flat with no variation. Writes come back in about 1.33 ms each (VolumeTotalWriteTime ÷ VolumeWriteOps), yet the queue holds about 1.33 requests on average. That matches what you'd expect at the cap: the application wants more IOPS than the volume will deliver, so requests wait in the queue and write latency goes up. The alarm (threshold 1) fired at 16:23:04. The instance layer is not the limit. The c6i.xlarge's EBS IOPS and throughput balances (EBSIOBalance% and EBSByteBalance%) stayed at 99% the whole time. The instance is doing about 1,500 IOPS against its roughly 10,000 IOPS baseline, and about 139 MB/s in total. Most of that 139 MB/s is about 131 MB/s of reads from another attached volume, gp3 vol-1234567890abcdef0_18, against a roughly 156 MB/s baseline. What to change: raise the provisioned IOPS on vol-0123456789abcdef0 with ModifyVolume, which works while the volume is attached. io2 allows up to 1,000 IOPS per GiB, so a 10 GiB volume can go as high as 10,000 IOPS. Pick a level above the application's real demand, for example 3,000–4,000 IOPS, rather than adding instance capacity. A caveat: the instance's EBS bandwidth is already about 89% used by the parallel gp3 read stream. Every extra 1,000 IOPS of 8 KiB writes adds about 8 MB/s, so above about 2,000–3,000 IOPS the instance's ~156 MB/s baseline becomes the next limit. If you plan to go higher, also throttle or move the large reads on vol-1234567890abcdef0_18, or move to a larger instance size with more EBS bandwidth. After a ModifyVolume, you must wait 6 hours before modifying the same volume again.
## Evidence
- CloudWatch alarm example-a-io2-queue-length went to ALARM at 2026-11-23 16:23:04 UTC: VolumeQueueLength was about 1.333 at 16:20, 16:21 and 16:22, above the threshold of 1.0.
- EC2 DescribeVolumes: vol-0123456789abcdef0 is io2, 10 GiB, provisioned at 1,000 IOPS, attached to i-1234567890abcdef0_3 as /dev/sdf.
- AWS/EBS VolumeWriteOps (5-minute sums): 0 from 15:50 to 16:10, 45,103 at 16:15, then 299,999 / 300,002 / 300,015 / 299,989 / 299,994 from 16:20 to 16:40. That is a flat 1,000 IOPS, equal to the provisioned limit.
- AWS/EBS VolumeWriteBytes: about 2.4576 GB per 5 minutes ÷ 300,000 writes ≈ 8 KiB per write, about 8.2 MB/s. Throughput is far too low to be the limit; the IOPS count is.
- AWS/EBS VolumeTotalWriteTime: about 400 s per 5 minutes ÷ 300,000 writes ≈ 1.33 ms per write. VolumeQueueLength averaged about 1.33–1.34 from 16:20 on, and was 0 before 16:15.
- AWS/EC2 EBSIOBalance% and EBSByteBalance% for i-1234567890abcdef0_3: minimum 99% from 15:50 to 16:45. The instance's EBS burst credits are not being used up.
- AWS/EC2 instance totals (5 minutes): EBSWriteOps about 300,350 plus EBSReadOps about 150,085, roughly 1,500 IOPS against the c6i.xlarge baseline of about 10,000. EBSReadBytes about 39.34 GB (≈131 MB/s) plus EBSWriteBytes about 2.46 GB (≈8 MB/s), roughly 139 MB/s against a ~156 MB/s baseline. That headroom is small but not yet exceeded.
- Alarm example-b-gp3-read-bytes has been in ALARM since 16:23:18 for vol-1234567890abcdef0_18 on the same instance, at about 7.87 GB of reads per minute. This is the parallel read stream that uses up most of the instance's EBS bandwidth.
## Affected resources
- vol-0123456789abcdef0 (io2, 1000 IOPS)
- i-1234567890abcdef0_3 (c6i.xlarge)
- vol-1234567890abcdef0_18 (gp3, concurrent read load sharing instance EBS bandwidth)
## Gaps
- VolumeIOPSExceededCheck and VolumeThroughputExceededCheck returned no datapoints, so the volume cap is inferred from VolumeWriteOps sitting exactly at the 1,000 IOPS limit.
- The c6i.xlarge EBS baselines (~10,000 IOPS, ~156 MB/s) are documented AWS figures and were not read through an API.
- There is no application-level or guest OS data (such as iostat or app latency logs) to measure the application's true IOPS demand or which process starts the 8 KiB writes at about 16:15.
- CloudTrail and deployment changes were not reviewed. There was no configuration change on the volume, so the trigger appears to be a change in workload.", "type": "text"}], "user_reference": null}

{"id": "17b4e4ae-eedf-4613-821c-1aadb79d7c99", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"thinking": "I can rule out the FIS experiments since they target a different volume. But the io2 volume shows VolumeIOPSExceededCheck firing from 16:15 onward, which directly confirms IOPS saturation — and I'm also noticing the actual instance baseline (6000 IOPS) doesn't match the 10,000 figure the fast report cited.

Working through the throughput math: the instance is at 89% of its 149 MiB/s baseline, with only ~16 MiB/s headroom. The other gp3 volume is separately saturated on throughput at its provisioned 125 MiB/s cap, while io2 itself has plenty of throughput headroom (7.81 of 256 MiB/s). Subtracting the other volumes' usage from the instance baseline leaves io2 only about 3,000 IOPS of room before throughput becomes the binding constraint rather than IOPS — so that's the real ceiling for any IOPS increase recommendation.

Checking queueing behavior: queue depth of ~1.33 with 1.33ms latency checks out via Little's Law, and that latency is notably above io2's sub-500µs expectation, which together with VolumeIOPSExceededCheck=1 confirms the volume is genuinely demand-constrained, not just coincidentally sitting at a round number.

Since io2 on c6i (Nitro) means Block Express, and true app demand beyond 3,000 IOPS is unknown, I'll recommend bumping to 3,000 now and flag that if the exceeded-check persists afterward, the next move is either reducing gp3-b's read throughput or resizing the instance to cover the combined demand — and I should correct that the old "6 hour wait" guidance for Elastic Volumes modifications is outdated, since the actual limit allows up to 4 modifications per rolling window.

I'm dropping the earlier fixed-wait claim entirely. On cost, io2 IOPS pricing scales up with provisioned IOPS-month, so I should note the rollback plan of reverting to 1,000 IOPS once the change completes. I'm also flagging that gp3-b is already throughput-capped at its provisioned 125 MiB/s with a queue length around 1.5, meaning raising its throughput would eat into the same instance headroom io2 needs — a direct conflict worth mentioning, alongside the timing detail that the workload jump to 751 IOPS on io2 and the gp3-b read activity both began at 16:19.

Given DescribeVolumesModifications returns NotFound for io2, there's never been a volume modification — so the trigger is purely an input change from a new in-guest workload, not infrastructure. I'm deciding to skip a CloudTrail check since it wouldn't capture in-guest activity anyway, and will just note it as a gap. Health checks come back clean (no open events, volume status OK, zero stalls), and the running FIS experiment targets a different volume entirely, ruling it out as a cause — pointing root cause back to the io2 volume's provisioned IOPS limit itself.

The provisioned 1,000 IOPS is the binding constraint, confirmed by VolumeIOPSExceededCheck and flat write IOPS at that cap since 16:19 — so the bottleneck is clearly at the Volume layer. I'll briefly note the EbsOptimized=false flag as a minor separate finding (though EbsOptimizedSupport defaults to always-on), and confirm sizing should use the c6i.xlarge's baseline throughput/IOPS rather than burst numbers per the skill's guidance. Now I'm moving to launch the mitigation proposal under the Limits category.

**Answer.** A new stream of 8 KiB writes started at 16:19 UTC and wants more than 1,000 IOPS. EBS has been flagging the limit as exceeded since then. The extra requests wait in the queue, which is the queue length the alarm caught and the higher write latency you're seeing. The instance still has some room, so changing the instance won't help yet.

**Evidence** (1-minute data unless noted; all times UTC on 2026-11-23)
- **Volume config:** vol-0123456789abcdef0 is io2, 10 GiB, provisioned at 1,000 IOPS. It has never been modified.
- **Onset:** 15:50–16:18 had no I/O at all (100% idle). The workload began at 16:19.
- **IOPS pinned at the limit:** from 16:20 to 16:47, writes held at 999.7–1,000.3 IOPS, reads at 0, average write size 8.0 KiB.
- **Direct signal:** EBS's own IOPS-exceeded check (`VolumeIOPSExceededCheck`) reads 1 in every 5-minute period from 16:15 to 16:45, and 0 before.
- **Queue and latency:** queue length (`VolumeQueueLength`) is 1.33–1.34, up from 0, and writes take about 1.33 ms each. The volume is almost never idle.
- **Throughput is not the limit:** it runs at 7.81 MiB/s against a limit of 256 MiB/s (0.256 MiB/s per provisioned IOPS). The throughput-exceeded check (`VolumeThroughputExceededCheck`) stayed at 0.
- **Instance layer has headroom:** the c6i.xlarge's sustained EBS limits are 6,000 IOPS and 156.25 MB/s (149.0 MiB/s), read from the API. All four attached volumes together do about 1,501 IOPS and 132.9 MiB/s (89%). Its EBS burst balances (`EBSIOBalance%` and `EBSByteBalance%`) stay at 99%, and CPU is about 1.2%.
- **No sign of an AWS-side problem:** the stalled-I/O check (`VolumeStalledIOCheck`) is 0 throughout. All four volumes report status ok. There are no open AWS Health events for EBS or EC2 in us-east-1.
- **Not a fault-injection test:** a FIS experiment (EXP1234567890abcdef_7, which adds EBS I/O latency) is running, but it targets a different volume, vol-1234567890abcdef0_11. It doesn't touch this instance.

**Binding layer:** Volume (provisioned IOPS).

**Recommendation:** raise the IOPS on vol-0123456789abcdef0 from 1,000 to 3,000 (`ModifyVolume`). This works while the volume stays attached, and the new IOPS take effect during the modification's `optimizing` phase.
- **How I got 3,000:** the instance can sustain 149.0 MiB/s. The other volumes are using 125.09 MiB/s, which leaves about 23.9 MiB/s. At 8 KiB per write that's about 3,060 IOPS, so throughput runs out before the instance's IOPS limit does. On IOPS, the total would be about 3,502 against 6,000.
- **Volume limits:** io2 allows up to 10,000 IOPS on 10 GiB, and at 3,000 IOPS the volume's throughput limit becomes 768 MiB/s.
- **Cost and rollback:** cost goes up with the provisioned IOPS. You can set it back to 1,000 once the modification completes. Each volume allows up to 4 modifications in any rolling 24 hours, and the next one can start as soon as the previous one finishes.
- **If the queue persists at 3,000:** if queue length stays high, or the IOPS-exceeded check still reads 1 at 3,000 IOPS, raising the volume further won't help. Either throttle or move the gp3 read stream, or move to an instance type with a higher sustained EBS limit.

I've started a separate mitigation proposal for this change.

**Separate findings**
- **The gp3 neighbour is also capped:** vol-1234567890abcdef0_18 has been reading at 125.07 MiB/s since 16:19, which is exactly its provisioned 125 MiB/s, with a queue length of 1.50–1.73. That stream takes most of the instance's EBS bandwidth. Raising that volume's throughput would use up the room the io2 volume needs.
- **Corrections to figures you may see elsewhere:**
  - The c6i.xlarge's sustained limit is 6,000 IOPS according to the API, not 10,000.
  - There is no fixed 6-hour wait between modifications.
  - 4,000 IOPS would be too high: it would need about 31.3 MiB/s of extra bandwidth and push the instance past its sustained limit.

**Gaps**
- I had no guest OS or application data, so I couldn't measure the workload's real IOPS demand or identify which process started writing at 16:19. 3,000 IOPS is a ceiling set by the instance, not a measured requirement.
- Metrics are 1-minute averages, so short spikes against the instance limit can't be ruled out. At 3,000 IOPS, sustained use would be about 148.5 of 149.0 MiB/s, which is very tight.

{"id": "7cbbebc9d73941ba986874fcf436fed6", "role": "user", "content": [{"text": "The background Task subagent assigned to task "propose-mitigation" successfully completed:

## Results
I recommend raising the provisioned IOPS on io2 volume `vol-0123456789abcdef0` from **1,000 to 3,000**. That is the highest value the instance can carry without hitting its own EBS limit. The change is online (no detach, no reboot) and the plan passed the safety validation. I have not applied it; it's for you to run.

## Mitigation summary

**Why:** Since 16:19 UTC a new 8 KiB write workload has been using all of the volume's 1,000 provisioned IOPS. From 16:20 to 16:47 writes stayed flat at 1,000 IOPS (7.81 MiB/s), the IOPS-exceeded check read 1 for every 5-minute period, and queue length sat around 1.33. That is what tripped the `example-a-io2-queue-length` alarm and raised write latency. Throughput is not the problem, and the investigation found no sign of an AWS-side fault.

**Why 3,000 and not more:**
- **The volume allows much more.** io2 permits up to 10,000 IOPS at 10 GiB, and 3,000 IOPS gives a throughput cap of about 768 MiB/s.
- **The instance is the real ceiling.** `i-1234567890abcdef0_3` (c6i.xlarge) has an EBS baseline of 6,000 IOPS and 149.0 MiB/s.
- **Another volume uses most of that.** `vol-1234567890abcdef0_18` (gp3) is reading at 125.07 MiB/s, leaving about 23.9 MiB/s for the io2 volume. At 8 KiB writes that is about 3,060 IOPS.
- **Instance IOPS has room.** The remaining IOPS headroom is about 5,498, so it doesn't limit this change.
- **Going higher has a cost.** Anything above 3,000 IOPS would hit the instance's throughput limit. You would first need to cut or move the gp3 read stream, or change to an instance type with a larger EBS baseline.

**Current state (read just now, this is the rollback baseline):** `vol-0123456789abcdef0` is io2, 10 GiB, 1,000 IOPS, in-use, attached to `i-1234567890abcdef0_3` as `/dev/sdf`, not multi-attach. The volume has never been modified.

## Execution plan

**1. Prepare**
- Save the current configuration as the rollback baseline. Expect io2 / 10 / 1000:
  `aws ec2 describe-volumes --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --query 'Volumes[0].{Type:VolumeType,Size:Size,Iops:Iops,State:State}' > vol-0123456789abcdef0-baseline.json`
- Take a backup snapshot before the change:
  `aws ec2 create-snapshot --region us-east-1 --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --description "Pre-IOPS-change backup of vol-0123456789abcdef0 (io2 10GiB 1000 IOPS)"`
  - The snapshot is a safety net only; you don't need to wait for it to complete. It adds a small storage charge, and changing IOPS does not put the data at risk.

**2. Pre-validate**
- Confirm no modification is already in progress:
  `aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0`
  - Proceed only if it returns NotFound or the latest `ModificationState` is `completed`.
  - Elastic Volumes allows up to 4 modifications per volume per rolling 24 hours. This change uses 1 and a rollback would use a second.

**3. Apply**
- Raise the provisioned IOPS to 3,000:
  `aws ec2 modify-volume --region us-east-1 --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --iops 3000`
  - **Cost:** this raises the monthly cost. 2,000 extra io2 IOPS is roughly +$130/month at us-east-1 list price; please check current pricing.
  - **Possible new ceiling:** combined with the gp3 reads, total instance throughput would get close to the 149.0 MiB/s baseline (about 125 + 23.4 MiB/s). If the write demand is above 3,000 IOPS, the bottleneck moves to the instance.
  - **When it takes effect:** the new IOPS apply once the modification reaches `optimizing`; you don't need to wait for `completed`.

**4. Post-validate**
- Watch the modification state:
  `aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --query 'VolumesModifications[0].{State:ModificationState,TargetIops:TargetIops,Progress:Progress}'`
  - Expect `TargetIops` 3000 and a state of `optimizing` or `completed`.
- Confirm the volume reports the new value:
  `aws ec2 describe-volumes --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --query 'Volumes[0].Iops'` (expect 3000)
- About 10–15 minutes after `optimizing`, check the volume metrics:
  `aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --region us-east-1 --namespace AWS/EBS --metric-name VolumeQueueLength --dimensions Name=VolumeId,Value=vol-0123456789abcdef0 --start-time <apply-time-minus-15m> --end-time <now> --period 60 --statistics Average`
  - Repeat with `--metric-name VolumeIOPSExceededCheck --period 300 --statistics Maximum` and `--metric-name VolumeWriteOps --period 60 --statistics Sum` (divide the sum by 60 to get IOPS).
  - **Healthy:** queue length below 1.0, IOPS-exceeded check at 0, and the alarm back to OK.
  - **Demand is above 3,000:** if write IOPS settle flat at about 3,000 and the IOPS-exceeded check stays at 1, the workload wants more than 3,000. See the follow-up options below.
- Check the instance-level limits:
  `aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --region us-east-1 --namespace AWS/EC2 --metric-name EBSByteBalance% --dimensions Name=InstanceId,Value=i-1234567890abcdef0_3 --start-time <apply-time-minus-15m> --end-time <now> --period 300 --statistics Minimum`
  - Repeat for `EBSIOBalance%`. Both should stay near 99%. A steady drop means the instance has become the bottleneck.

**5. Rollback** (only if needed, and only after the previous modification has left `modifying`)
- Restore the original IOPS:
  `aws ec2 modify-volume --region us-east-1 --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --iops 1000`
  - This counts as another of the 4 modifications allowed per 24 hours.
  - Rolling back brings the original problem back: queue length above 1 and higher write latency.
  - Confirm with `describe-volumes-modifications` (`TargetIops` 1000).

## Follow-up options if 3,000 IOPS is not enough (not part of this plan)
- **Reduce or move the gp3 read stream.** The reads on `vol-1234567890abcdef0_18` started at the same minute as the writes. Cutting, rescheduling or moving them frees instance throughput for io2.
- **Change the instance type.** A type with a larger EBS baseline lets you go above about 3,000 IOPS. That needs a stop/start, so it is a planned change, not an incident fix.

## Code / configuration change (stops the fix being undone)
- **Update the infrastructure-as-code definition.** Set `vol-0123456789abcdef0` (tag Name `example-a-io2`, Project `example`) to `Iops: 3000`, or to the value that post-validation proves is needed, so a later deploy doesn't put it back to 1,000.
  - Done when: the deployed config matches the live volume, a plan/diff shows no change, and a sizing note records the constraint (io2 IOPS × 8 KiB + other attached volume throughput ≤ 149.0 MiB/s on c6i.xlarge).
- **Add an alarm on the IOPS-exceeded check** for this volume (`VolumeIOPSExceededCheck` ≥ 1 for 2 consecutive 5-minute periods), alongside the queue-length alarm.
  - Done when: the alarm exists in code and fires in a test when IOPS is saturated.

## What I could not cover
- **True demand is unknown.** There is no guest-OS or application data, so 3,000 IOPS is the safest ceiling for this instance, not a measured requirement.
- **The workload source is unidentified.** I don't know which process started the 8 KiB writes (or the gp3 reads) at 16:19, so I could not judge whether the demand is legitimate or a runaway job. If it isn't legitimate, reducing it is cheaper than buying IOPS.
- **No deployment history found.** I didn't find any pipeline or deployment link for this resource, so the plan uses manual AWS CLI commands.

# Investigation Summary

## Symptoms

### VolumeQueueLength above threshold on example-a-io2
**Description:** Alarm example-a-io2-queue-length ([redacted ARN]) entered ALARM at 2026-11-23 16:23:04 UTC. Average VolumeQueueLength over 60s periods was 1.335, 1.333 and 1.333 at 16:20, 16:21 and 16:22, all above the 1.0 threshold. The volume is vol-0123456789abcdef0. The alarm has no actions configured.
**Time:** 2026-11-23T16:19:00Z

## Findings

### Root Cause: io2 volume's 1,000 provisioned IOPS too low for the new 8 KiB write load
**Description:** A new stream of 8 KiB writes started at 16:19 UTC on vol-0123456789abcdef0 (io2, 10 GiB, 1,000 IOPS, never modified; [redacted ARN]). Writes are pinned at 999.7–1,000.3 IOPS, and VolumeIOPSExceededCheck = 1 from 16:15. The extra requests queue up (VolumeQueueLength 1.33–1.34, ~1.33 ms writes), so the alarm fired at 16:23:04. Throughput is not the limit: 7.81 of 256 MiB/s, and VolumeThroughputExceededCheck = 0. The instance layer also has headroom: 1,501 of 6,000 IOPS, 132.9 of 149.0 MiB/s, EBS balances 99%, CPU ~1.2%. Nothing points to an AWS-side problem or the FIS experiment. The binding layer is the volume's provisioned IOPS.
**Cascades to:** symptom-io2-queue-length

#### Supporting Observations
- **io2 write IOPS flat at 1000 since 16:20:** vol-0123456789abcdef0 went from idle (0 ops, 100% idle) to 752 write IOPS at 16:19 and has held at ~1000 write IOPS (exactly the provisioned 1000) since 16:20. Writes are 8 KiB, ~7.8 MiB/s, with ~1.33 ms write latency. Idle time is ~0% and there are no reads. Queue length matches at ~1.33.
- **VolumeIOPSExceededCheck = 1 on io2 volume since 16:15:** On vol-0123456789abcdef0, VolumeIOPSExceededCheck changed from 0 to 1 at 16:15 and has stayed at 1. That means the workload is asking for more than the provisioned 1000 IOPS. VolumeThroughputExceededCheck stayed at 0 throughout. At the instance level, i-1234567890abcdef0_3 is doing ~1501 IOPS and ~132.9 MiB/s (~139 MB/s), against a baseline of 6000 IOPS and 156.25 MB/s. The gp3 volume vol-1234567890abcdef0_18 also has a queue of ~1.5–1.7.
- **No instance-level EBS bottleneck:** For i-1234567890abcdef0_3, EBSIOBalance% and EBSByteBalance% held at 99% from 16:15 to 16:47, and CPU was ~1.2%. On vol-0123456789abcdef0, VolumeStalledIOCheck was 0 and VolumeThroughputPercentage was 100%. VolumeAvgWriteLatency was ~1.33 ms from 16:19 onward.
- **All four attached volumes report status ok:** describe_volume_status shows io-enabled passed and io-performance normal for vol-0123456789abcdef0, vol-1234567890abcdef0_18, vol-1234567890abcdef0_15 and vol-1234567890abcdef0_19. No events or actions are scheduled.
- **FIS experiments target a different volume:** Both FIS experiments use template EXT1234567890abcdef_4 (example scenario d, 500 ms EBS I/O latency). Their only target is vol-1234567890abcdef0_11, which is not one of the volumes attached to i-1234567890abcdef0_3. EXP1234567890abcdef_4 ran from 16:15:47 to 16:19:24 and was stopped by a user. EXP1234567890abcdef_7 has been running since 16:47:16. Neither experiment touches vol-0123456789abcdef0, so they don't explain the queue-length alarm.
- **No AWS Health events and no volume modifications:** AWS Health has no open or upcoming EBS/EC2 events in us-east-1. describe_volumes_modifications returns no modification history for vol-0123456789abcdef0 or vol-1234567890abcdef0_19.

#### Gaps
- **No guest OS or application data:** Without in-guest or application telemetry, the workload's real IOPS demand could not be measured, and the process that started writing at 16:19 could not be identified. The 3,000 IOPS figure is a ceiling set by the instance's bandwidth, not a measured requirement.
- **1-minute metric resolution:** With 1-minute averages, short spikes against the instance's sustained EBS limit cannot be ruled out. At 3,000 IOPS, sustained use would be ~148.5 of 149.0 MiB/s.

# Mitigation Summary

## Action
Raise provisioned IOPS on io2 volume vol-0123456789abcdef0 from 1,000 to 3,000 (online ModifyVolume, no detach or reboot)

## Reasoning
Since 16:19 UTC a new 8 KiB write workload has used all 1,000 provisioned IOPS: writes sit flat at 1,000 IOPS, VolumeIOPSExceededCheck = 1 and queue length is ~1.33. 3,000 IOPS is the ceiling the c6i.xlarge can carry. Its 149.0 MiB/s EBS baseline minus the 125.07 MiB/s gp3 read stream on vol-1234567890abcdef0_18 leaves ~23.9 MiB/s, which is ~3,060 IOPS at 8 KiB. Going higher needs the gp3 reads reduced or moved, or a larger instance type.

## Execution Plan

### Step 1: Prepare

#### 1.1 Record the current config (expect io2 / 10 / 1000) as the rollback…
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volumes --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --query 'Volumes[0].{Type:VolumeType,Size:Size,Iops:Iops,State:State}' > vol-0123456789abcdef0-baseline.json
```
**Purpose:** Record the current config (expect io2 / 10 / 1000) as the rollback baseline

#### 1.2 Take a safety-net snapshot before the change
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 create-snapshot --region us-east-1 --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --description "Pre-IOPS-change backup of vol-0123456789abcdef0 (io2 10GiB 1000 IOPS)"
```
**Purpose:** Take a safety-net snapshot before the change
**Risks:** Small snapshot storage charge
**Advisory:** No need to wait for the snapshot to complete; changing IOPS does not put data at risk

### Step 2: Pre Validate

#### 2.1 Proceed only if the result is NotFound or the latest ModificationState…
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0
```
**Purpose:** Proceed only if the result is NotFound or the latest ModificationState is completed
**Advisory:** Up to 4 modifications per volume per rolling 24 h; this change uses 1 and a rollback would use another

### Step 3: Apply

#### 3.1 Lift the volume's IOPS ceiling above the write demand
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 modify-volume --region us-east-1 --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --iops 3000
```
**Purpose:** Lift the volume's IOPS ceiling above the write demand
**Risks:** About +$130/month for 2,000 extra io2 IOPS (us-east-1 list price), Total instance throughput nears the 149.0 MiB/s baseline (~125 + 23.4 MiB/s)
**Advisory:** The new IOPS apply once the modification reaches optimizing; no need to wait for completed, If demand is above 3,000 IOPS, the bottleneck moves to the instance

### Step 4: Post Validate

#### 4.1 Confirm TargetIops is 3000 and the state is optimizing or completed
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --query 'VolumesModifications[0].{State:ModificationState,TargetIops:TargetIops,Progress:Progress}'
```
**Purpose:** Confirm TargetIops is 3000 and the state is optimizing or completed

#### 4.2 Confirm the volume reports 3000 IOPS
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volumes --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --query 'Volumes[0].Iops'
```
**Purpose:** Confirm the volume reports 3000 IOPS

#### 4.3 Check that queue length drops below 1.0 about 10–15 min after optimizing
**Type:** command
```
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --region us-east-1 --namespace AWS/EBS --metric-name VolumeQueueLength --dimensions Name=VolumeId,Value=vol-0123456789abcdef0 --start-time <apply-time-minus-15m> --end-time <now> --period 60 --statistics Average
```
**Purpose:** Check that queue length drops below 1.0 about 10–15 min after optimizing
**Advisory:** Repeat for VolumeIOPSExceededCheck (period 300, Maximum; expect 0) and VolumeWriteOps (period 60, Sum ÷ 60 = IOPS), If write IOPS sit flat at ~3,000 with the IOPS-exceeded check still at 1, demand exceeds 3,000; reduce or move the gp3 reads, or change the instance type

#### 4.4 Confirm the instance has not become the bottleneck (balance stays near…
**Type:** command
```
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --region us-east-1 --namespace AWS/EC2 --metric-name EBSByteBalance% --dimensions Name=InstanceId,Value=i-1234567890abcdef0_3 --start-time <apply-time-minus-15m> --end-time <now> --period 300 --statistics Minimum
```
**Purpose:** Confirm the instance has not become the bottleneck (balance stays near 99%)
**Advisory:** Repeat for EBSIOBalance%; a steady drop means the instance limit is now binding

### Step 5: Rollback

#### 5.1 Return the volume to its original provisioned IOPS
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 modify-volume --region us-east-1 --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --iops 1000
```
**Purpose:** Return the volume to its original provisioned IOPS
**Risks:** Brings back queue length above 1 and higher write latency, Uses another of the 4 modifications allowed per 24 h
**Advisory:** Run only after the previous modification has left modifying; confirm TargetIops 1000 with describe-volumes-modifications

## Code Change Specification

### Requirements

#### 1. Codify the new IOPS in infrastructure-as-code
**Description:** Set vol-0123456789abcdef0 (Name example-a-io2, Project example) to Iops: 3000, or to the value post-validation proves is needed, so a later deploy does not revert it to 1,000.
**Acceptance Criteria:**
- Deployed config matches the live volume
- Plan/diff shows no change
- A sizing note records the constraint: io2 IOPS × 8 KiB + other attached volume throughput ≤ 149.0 MiB/s on c6i.xlarge

#### 2. Alarm on IOPS saturation
**Description:** Add an alarm on VolumeIOPSExceededCheck ≥ 1 for 2 consecutive 5-minute periods for this volume, alongside the queue-length alarm.
**Acceptance Criteria:**
- The alarm exists in code
- The alarm fires in a test when IOPS is saturated

     2	name: storage-ebs-expertise
     3	description: >
     4	  Use this skill when a user wants to know why Amazon EBS storage is slow, why an
     5	  EBS alarm fired, or whether their EBS setup is production-ready, even if they only

     11	  IOPS or throughput changes; for requests to raise IOPS or modify a volume; for a
     12	  volume modification that looks stuck or failed; for deciding which snapshots or

     17	metadata:
     18	  author: dewavic
     19	  version: "1.0.0"
     20	  summary: "Troubleshoot Amazon EBS performance, volume modifications, snapshots, encryption, quotas and cost, and review an account's EBS setup with read-only checks."
     21	  aws-devops-agent-skills.agent-types: "CHAT, INCIDENT_RCA"
     22	  aws-devops-agent-skills.aws-services: "Amazon EBS, Amazon EC2, Amazon CloudWatch, AWS CloudTrail, AWS Service Quotas"
     23	  aws-devops-agent-skills.technical-domains: "Storage"
     24	---
     25	# Amazon EBS Expertise
     26	
     27	Use this skill to troubleshoot Amazon EBS problems and to review an account's Amazon EBS setup. It has two modes. Troubleshoot mode answers "something is wrong, why?" through one of five paths and returns a fixed verdict. Review mode answers "is my EBS setup healthy before something goes wrong?" and returns a rated report. Both modes are read-only and share the same volume-type rules, instance limits and service rules. Load only the reference files the request needs.
     28	
     29	## When to Use This Skill
     30	
     31	- Storage-related slowness, timeouts or high I/O latency on an Amazon EC2 instance.
     32	- An alarm on AWS/EBS metrics or on instance `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%`.
     33	- A request to raise IOPS or throughput, or to modify a volume.
     34	- A volume modification that looks stuck, failed, or did not improve performance.
     35	- Snapshot, AMI, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, AWS Backup or Recycle Bin questions, including which snapshots need owner review before deletion.
     36	- Encrypted-volume access errors and AWS KMS questions for Amazon EBS.
     37	- Amazon EBS cost increases, idle or over-provisioned volumes.
     38	- An operation that failed on an Amazon EBS quota, or "how close am I to my limits?"
     39	- A request to review Amazon EBS posture before a launch, migration or peak event.
     40	
     41	Do not use this skill for Amazon S3, Amazon EFS, Amazon FSx, instance store, or Amazon EC2 issues unrelated to Amazon EBS.
     42	
     43	## Prerequisites
     44	
     45	- Read-only permissions for the APIs listed in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md).
     46	- AWS CloudTrail access is optional. The skill works without it.
     47	- Mutating changes run only through directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App), which need their own role and operator approval on the approval card.
     48	
     49	---
     50	
     51	## Workflow
     52	
     53	Copy this checklist and tick each step as you finish it:
     54	
     55	- [ ] Step 1: Classify the request
     56	- [ ] Step 2: Load the shared references
     57	- [ ] Step 3: Run the path and draft the report
     58	- [ ] Step 4: Check the draft, fix it, then present it
     59	
     60	## Step 1: Classify the Request
     61	
     62	| The user says or the alarm shows | Mode and path | Load |
     63	|---|---|---|
     64	| "My app is slow", high latency, an alarm on AWS/EBS metrics, `EBSIOBalance%` or `EBSByteBalance%`, "is it storage?", "how much IOPS do I need?" | Troubleshoot: performance | [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md) |
     65	| "My modification is stuck", "the new IOPS has not taken effect", a `ModifyVolume` error, resize, gp2 to gp3, extend the file system, shrink or cancel | Troubleshoot: volume modification | [references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md](references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md) |
     66	| "Which snapshots can I delete?", snapshot copy did not arrive, AMI creation stuck, recover a deleted snapshot or volume, Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, Recycle Bin | Troubleshoot: snapshots | [references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md](references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md) |
     67	| "I can't attach my KMS-encrypted volume", share an encrypted snapshot or AMI, encryption by default, re-encrypt a volume | Troubleshoot: encryption | [references/troubleshoot-encryption.md](references/troubleshoot-encryption.md) |
     68	| "Why did my EBS bill go up?", unexplained charges, idle or unattached volumes, pricing model | Troubleshoot: billing | [references/troubleshoot-billing.md](references/troubleshoot-billing.md) |
     69	| "Limit exceeded", a quota error, "how close am I to my limits?" | Shared capability: quota headroom | [Capacity and quota headroom](references/review-operational.md#capacity-and-quota-headroom) |
     70	| "Are my volumes backed up?" | Review: resilience area | [Resilience](references/review-operational.md#resilience) |
     71	| "Review my EBS setup", "is my storage production-ready?" | Review | [references/review-operational.md](references/review-operational.md) and [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md) |
     72	
     73	If a request fits more than one row, answer the question the user asked first and treat the rest as Separate findings.
     74	
     75	## Step 2: Load the Shared References
     76	
     77	- Always load [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md) (read-only APIs, metric math, errors and fallbacks).
     78	- Load [references/metrics-thresholds.md](references/metrics-thresholds.md) for any metric judgement.
     79	- Load [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md) for the verdict, the binding layer, escalation and review ratings.
     80	- Load [references/ebs-best-practices.md](references/ebs-best-practices.md) for service rules (Elastic Volumes, instance limits, quotas, snapshots, quirks).
     81	
     82	## Step 3: Run the Path and Draft the Report
     83	
     84	Follow the numbered procedure in the loaded path. Discover every value from the APIs. Then draft the report in the format below.
     85	
     86	### Troubleshoot verdict format
     87	
     88	1. **Answer:** the asked question, answered first.
     89	2. **Evidence:** values with units and time window.
     90	3. **Binding layer:** Volume, Instance, Burst credits, Quota, Not EBS, AWS-side impairment (only with a direct signal, see [references/finding-logic.md](references/finding-logic.md)), Indeterminate, or Not applicable.
     91	4. **Recommendation:** exact parameters, or "No change".
     92	5. **Separate findings:** other true facts that do not change the Answer.
     93	6. **Gaps:** what could not be checked and why.
     94	
     95	In an investigation, put the Answer and the Recommendation with its exact parameters in the root cause finding, not only under Gaps. Keep the findings on the resource the user asked about. Mention another volume only when it shares the same instance EBS baseline, and then as a Separate finding.
     96	
     97	When the Binding layer is Indeterminate, report it as one finding. Do not offer AWS-side impairment as a hypothesis. List each direct check you ran (volume status, `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, AWS Health, AWS FIS) with its result as supporting evidence, say that no check confirms or rules out an EBS-side slowdown, and give the escalation path.
     98	
     99	Review mode uses the rated report in [references/review-report-format.md](references/review-report-format.md). Every Review mode response MUST begin with its Summary table, which rates all six areas (capacity and quota headroom, observability, cost hygiene, resilience, encryption posture, deletion protection), even when an area has no findings or is `Indeterminate`. The Summary table is required, not optional. Do not open with prose or an offer to run the review; start with the table, then the per-area detail.
     100	
     101	## Step 4: Check the Draft Before Presenting It
     102	
     103	Review the draft from Step 3 against these checks. Fix anything that fails, then present it.
     104	
     105	- Every number under Evidence came from an API call made in this session, has its unit and time window, and matches the resource ID it is attributed to.
     106	- The Binding layer agrees with the Evidence: the named layer is the one at its limit, and the other layers were checked and shown to have headroom. The Evidence gives the instance EBS baseline in MiB/s and IOPS next to the summed demand of all attached volumes.
     107	- Any Recommendation stays within the instance's EBS baseline and the volume type's documented limits, and it is not more provisioning for an impairment.
     108	- Every snapshot tier is backed by the checks it requires; if one of those checks failed, the item is not listed for owner review. No snapshot is recommended for deletion; the owner confirms first.
     109	- A review answer starts with the Summary table and rates all six areas.
     110	- Every API that failed or was not called is listed under Gaps.
     111	
     112	---
     113	
     114	## Critical Rules
     115	
     116	- **Read-only.** Changes (ModifyVolume, quota requests) are proposed with exact parameters, cost and rollback, and run only through operator-approved directed actions (Agent Actions in the Operator Web App). Approval is given only on the approval card. A typed "approve" in chat is not approval.
     117	- **Deletes are manual customer steps.** AWS DevOps Agent refuses delete-class operations (for example DeleteSnapshot, DeleteVolume, DeregisterImage), so never propose them as directed actions. After the owner confirms they no longer need the resource, give the commands for the customer to run with their own credentials.
     118	- **Answer in one reply.** In chat, run the checks in this conversation and return the finished verdict or report as your reply. Do not hand the work to a background sub-agent and reply with a "started" or "I will report back" message, because that message becomes the answer the user sees first.
     119	- **Discover, don't assume:** read every configuration value from the APIs.
     120	- **Rule EBS in or out before tuning it.**
     121	- **Answer the asked question first;** other findings go under "Separate findings".
     122	- **Review mode starts with the Summary table.** Every Review mode response begins with the Summary table of all six rated areas. The table is required, not optional.
     123	- **Always check the instance layer** and size changes within the instance's EBS **baseline**.
     124	- **Never recommend more provisioning for an impairment.**
     125	- **Use current service rules:** up to 4 Elastic Volumes modifications per volume per rolling 24 hours. There is no fixed waiting period between modifications; the next one is allowed once the previous one completes.
     126	- **No interpretation without data:** report what couldn't be checked and use fallbacks. `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the most recent modification per volume; modification history and counts come from the optional AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` events, or are listed under Gaps.
     127	- **Units:** MiB/s for throughput, stated every time.
     128	- **Escalate** on scope signals or when the investigation can't explain the symptom.
     129	
     130	## Gotchas
     131	
     132	- A modification in `optimizing` is not stuck. The new size, IOPS or throughput already applies while it optimizes.
     133	- `DescribeInstanceTypes` reports EBS bandwidth in MB/s. Convert it to MiB/s before comparing it with volume throughput.
     134	- On io1 and io2, `VolumeThroughputPercentage` is the percentage of provisioned IOPS delivered. It is not a throughput signal.
     135	- `VolumeAvgIOPS`, `VolumeAvgThroughput`, `VolumeAvgReadLatency` and `VolumeAvgWriteLatency` need both `VolumeId` and `InstanceId` and exist only on Nitro instances. `VolumeAvgThroughput` is in KiB/s. `VolumeTotalReadTime` and `VolumeTotalWriteTime` are in seconds.
     136	- Rising latency and queue length with falling IOPS is not proof of an AWS-side impairment. Without a direct signal (failed `VolumeStalledIOCheck`, impaired volume status, or an open AWS Health event) and without a running AWS FIS experiment, the Binding layer is Indeterminate.
     137	- `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the latest modification per volume. It cannot count modifications in the last 24 hours.
     138	- `ListRecoveryPointsByResource` without `ManagedByAWSBackupOnly` set to true also lists snapshots that AWS Backup did not create.
     139	- A snapshot whose source volume is gone may be the only remaining copy of the data. List it for owner review; never call it safe to delete.
     140	- Snapshots are incremental, so deleting one may free less storage than its size suggests.
     141	
     142	## Error Handling
     143	
     144	Errors, gated reads and missing metrics are handled with the fallback table in [references/data-collection.md](references/data-collection.md). Name every failed API under Gaps and continue with the rest.
     145	
     146	## References

     148	- [references/troubleshoot-performance.md](references/troubleshoot-performance.md): performance attribution, the live-tested procedure
     149	- [references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md](references/troubleshoot-snapshots.md): snapshot tiers (owner review), copy, AMI, lifecycle and recovery
     150	- [references/troubleshoot-encryption.md](references/troubleshoot-encryption.md): AWS KMS access, sharing encrypted snapshots, default encryption
     151	- [references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md](references/troubleshoot-volume-modification.md): modification states, limits, errors, sizing, file system extension
     152	- [references/troubleshoot-billing.md](references/troubleshoot-billing.md): cost breakdown, change records, right-sizing
     153	- [references/review-operational.md](references/review-operational.md): Review mode checks and the quota headroom capability

{"id": "a0946696-4be3-44da-931b-500237fe87ee", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "I recommend raising the provisioned IOPS on io2 volume `vol-0123456789abcdef0` from **1,000 to 3,000**. That is the highest value the instance can carry without hitting its own EBS limit. The change is online (no detach, no reboot) and the plan passed the safety validation. I have not applied it; it's for you to run.

## Mitigation summary

**Why:** Since 16:19 UTC a new 8 KiB write workload has been using all of the volume's 1,000 provisioned IOPS. From 16:20 to 16:47 writes stayed flat at 1,000 IOPS (7.81 MiB/s), the IOPS-exceeded check read 1 for every 5-minute period, and queue length sat around 1.33. That is what tripped the `example-a-io2-queue-length` alarm and raised write latency. Throughput is not the problem, and the investigation found no sign of an AWS-side fault.

**Why 3,000 and not more:**
- **The volume allows much more.** io2 permits up to 10,000 IOPS at 10 GiB, and 3,000 IOPS gives a throughput cap of about 768 MiB/s.
- **The instance is the real ceiling.** `i-1234567890abcdef0_3` (c6i.xlarge) has an EBS baseline of 6,000 IOPS and 149.0 MiB/s.
- **Another volume uses most of that.** `vol-1234567890abcdef0_18` (gp3) is reading at 125.07 MiB/s, leaving about 23.9 MiB/s for the io2 volume. At 8 KiB writes that is about 3,060 IOPS.
- **Instance IOPS has room.** The remaining IOPS headroom is about 5,498, so it doesn't limit this change.
- **Going higher has a cost.** Anything above 3,000 IOPS would hit the instance's throughput limit. You would first need to cut or move the gp3 read stream, or change to an instance type with a larger EBS baseline.

**Current state (read just now, this is the rollback baseline):** `vol-0123456789abcdef0` is io2, 10 GiB, 1,000 IOPS, in-use, attached to `i-1234567890abcdef0_3` as `/dev/sdf`, not multi-attach. The volume has never been modified.

## Execution plan

**1. Prepare**
- Save the current configuration as the rollback baseline. Expect io2 / 10 / 1000:
  `aws ec2 describe-volumes --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --query 'Volumes[0].{Type:VolumeType,Size:Size,Iops:Iops,State:State}' > vol-0123456789abcdef0-baseline.json`
- Take a backup snapshot before the change:
  `aws ec2 create-snapshot --region us-east-1 --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --description "Pre-IOPS-change backup of vol-0123456789abcdef0 (io2 10GiB 1000 IOPS)"`
  - The snapshot is a safety net only; you don't need to wait for it to complete. It adds a small storage charge, and changing IOPS does not put the data at risk.

**2. Pre-validate**
- Confirm no modification is already in progress:
  `aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0`
  - Proceed only if it returns NotFound or the latest `ModificationState` is `completed`.
  - Elastic Volumes allows up to 4 modifications per volume per rolling 24 hours. This change uses 1 and a rollback would use a second.

**3. Apply**
- Raise the provisioned IOPS to 3,000:
  `aws ec2 modify-volume --region us-east-1 --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --iops 3000`
  - **Cost:** this raises the monthly cost. 2,000 extra io2 IOPS is roughly +$130/month at us-east-1 list price; please check current pricing.
  - **Possible new ceiling:** combined with the gp3 reads, total instance throughput would get close to the 149.0 MiB/s baseline (about 125 + 23.4 MiB/s). If the write demand is above 3,000 IOPS, the bottleneck moves to the instance.
  - **When it takes effect:** the new IOPS apply once the modification reaches `optimizing`; you don't need to wait for `completed`.

**4. Post-validate**
- Watch the modification state:
  `aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --query 'VolumesModifications[0].{State:ModificationState,TargetIops:TargetIops,Progress:Progress}'`
  - Expect `TargetIops` 3000 and a state of `optimizing` or `completed`.
- Confirm the volume reports the new value:
  `aws ec2 describe-volumes --region us-east-1 --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --query 'Volumes[0].Iops'` (expect 3000)
- About 10–15 minutes after `optimizing`, check the volume metrics:
  `aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --region us-east-1 --namespace AWS/EBS --metric-name VolumeQueueLength --dimensions Name=VolumeId,Value=vol-0123456789abcdef0 --start-time <apply-time-minus-15m> --end-time <now> --period 60 --statistics Average`
  - Repeat with `--metric-name VolumeIOPSExceededCheck --period 300 --statistics Maximum` and `--metric-name VolumeWriteOps --period 60 --statistics Sum` (divide the sum by 60 to get IOPS).
  - **Healthy:** queue length below 1.0, IOPS-exceeded check at 0, and the alarm back to OK.
  - **Demand is above 3,000:** if write IOPS settle flat at about 3,000 and the IOPS-exceeded check stays at 1, the workload wants more than 3,000. See the follow-up options below.
- Check the instance-level limits:
  `aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --region us-east-1 --namespace AWS/EC2 --metric-name EBSByteBalance% --dimensions Name=InstanceId,Value=i-1234567890abcdef0_3 --start-time <apply-time-minus-15m> --end-time <now> --period 300 --statistics Minimum`
  - Repeat for `EBSIOBalance%`. Both should stay near 99%. A steady drop means the instance has become the bottleneck.

**5. Rollback** (only if needed, and only after the previous modification has left `modifying`)
- Restore the original IOPS:
  `aws ec2 modify-volume --region us-east-1 --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --iops 1000`
  - This counts as another of the 4 modifications allowed per 24 hours.
  - Rolling back brings the original problem back: queue length above 1 and higher write latency.
  - Confirm with `describe-volumes-modifications` (`TargetIops` 1000).

## Follow-up options if 3,000 IOPS is not enough (not part of this plan)
- **Reduce or move the gp3 read stream.** The reads on `vol-1234567890abcdef0_18` started at the same minute as the writes. Cutting, rescheduling or moving them frees instance throughput for io2.
- **Change the instance type.** A type with a larger EBS baseline lets you go above about 3,000 IOPS. That needs a stop/start, so it is a planned change, not an incident fix.

## Code / configuration change (stops the fix being undone)
- **Update the infrastructure-as-code definition.** Set `vol-0123456789abcdef0` (tag Name `example-a-io2`, Project `example`) to `Iops: 3000`, or to the value that post-validation proves is needed, so a later deploy doesn't put it back to 1,000.
  - Done when: the deployed config matches the live volume, a plan/diff shows no change, and a sizing note records the constraint (io2 IOPS × 8 KiB + other attached volume throughput ≤ 149.0 MiB/s on c6i.xlarge).
- **Add an alarm on the IOPS-exceeded check** for this volume (`VolumeIOPSExceededCheck` ≥ 1 for 2 consecutive 5-minute periods), alongside the queue-length alarm.
  - Done when: the alarm exists in code and fires in a test when IOPS is saturated.

## What I could not cover
- **True demand is unknown.** There is no guest-OS or application data, so 3,000 IOPS is the safest ceiling for this instance, not a measured requirement.
- **The workload source is unidentified.** I don't know which process started the 8 KiB writes (or the gp3 reads) at 16:19, so I could not judge whether the demand is legitimate or a runaway job. If it isn't legitimate, reducing it is cheaper than buying IOPS.
- **No deployment history found.** I didn't find any pipeline or deployment link for this resource, so the plan uses manual AWS CLI commands.", "type": "text"}], "user_reference": null}
